Brainstead keeps it in the Keychain (platform module), refreshes it itself, and syncs: new messages in chats the user picks, meeting transcripts for meetings the user was invited to (found through the calendar), and new mail in the Inbox. Each item is saved through the extensions' capture path, so the Inbox and Ingest new sources as they arrive work unchanged. Today shows upcoming meetings from the calendar. The sync only ever reads: no sends, edits or read-state changes, although the tokens would allow them. Internal Teams endpoints and Outlook REST are not Graph, so the no-Graph rule stands.
title: Teams and Outlook sync reuses the web apps' sign-in, handed over by the extensions

consequences: A chat's messages reach the vault up to a day late, in exchange for one ingest per chat per day. A message edited or added to an earlier day after its source was written isn't synced again. The ignore list lives in settings, so it's per machine.
context: D-20261025-01 lets Brainstead read Teams and Outlook itself. Every source is ingested when Ingest new sources as they arrive is on, so how items are grouped decides the cost and the noise. Agreed with the user 2026-10-25.
decision: Chats: every 1:1 and group chat, one source per chat per day, written once the day ends or the chat has been quiet for a few hours. Channel posts: off by default; the user ticks channels in Settings; one source per thread per day. Meeting chats: folded into the same source as the meeting's transcript, not their own. Transcripts: for meetings in the user's calendar, fetched after the meeting ends. Mail: new Inbox threads, skipping mail Outlook puts under Other and senders or domains on an ignore list; Don't sync this sender (sender or domain) on a synced email in the Inbox and Sources, with a key and an MCP tool, and the list editable in Settings. Today shows upcoming meetings from the calendar. The capture extensions stay for capturing anything by hand.
title: What Teams and Outlook sync captures, and how it's grouped

consequences: A new chat added later also respects the cap on first encounter, so it can't flood either. Mail is bounded to the newest MAIL_TOP (40) per pass regardless. The cap is a local setting.
context: First live run pulled 454 chat-days + 40 emails into the Inbox at once; fine for this user but a big mailbox or long chat history could flood someone. Also wanted Today to look ahead. Refines D-20261025-02.
decision: Settings › Teams and Outlook sync has 'On first sync, load the last N days' (syncInitialDays, default 7, 0 = no limit). The cap applies the first time each chat is seen (older days are marked done so they're never backfilled) and on the first mail run; after that the sync is purely incremental. Today's Upcoming meetings card shows the rest of today, and from 12:00 local also tomorrow's under a Tomorrow heading.
title: Teams and Outlook sync: first-sync history cap and Today's tomorrow meetings

consequences: Reuses fetch/deliver/state, so it can't drift from the background sync. The menu labels for Don't sync this sender/domain were shortened to one line (the address goes in the tooltip) after they wrapped. pull_teams_outlook added to core MCP_TOOLS.
context: User wants to ask an assistant to gather a topic's recent emails, chats and transcripts and write a summary note, reusing already-synced sources and pulling only what's missing. Builds on D-20261025-01/-02/-03.
decision: New MCP tool pull_teams_outlook(query, days=7, kinds) and command sync_pull: gathers matching chats (local term match over a day's messages + topic), mail (Outlook $search, or recent Inbox when no query), and meeting transcripts (calendar subjects) over the window into sources/ via the shared capture path, and returns each source's kind/title/date/path. Sync state now also stores the written path per chat-day, mail id and meeting (backward-compatible added maps), so an already-pulled item is vended by path rather than re-fetched; items pulled before this (no stored path) are reported as already-in-vault for the assistant to find with search. Reads only; macOS only; needs sync on and signed in.
title: On-demand pull from Teams and Outlook for assistants (pull_teams_outlook)

consequences: No real US-timezone bug existed; the app always used the Mac's local time — the Inbox was just showing capture time. Items synced before itemDate existed keep showing capture time until re-pulled. Meeting chat fetch fails soft (empty) so it never blocks the transcript.
context: Implements the meeting-chat half of D-20261025-02 (recorded but unbuilt), and fixes the Inbox showing capture time for synced items.
decision: transcript_capture now also fetches the meeting conversation's chat messages (chatsvc, the meeting thread id) and appends them to the transcript Thread after an 'In-meeting chat' divider message, so a meeting note sees both. Captured gained itemDate (RFC3339): the sync/pull set it to a chat's last message time, a mail's received time, or a meeting's start, and the Inbox dates the row by it (local time) rather than the capture time. Chat sources are named by the conversation day (meeting_date on the chat capture, used by render) and a 1:1 day where only the user wrote is titled by the partner. The on-demand pull re-fetches a source whose recorded file is missing (user deleted it).
title: Fold the meeting chat into the transcript source; date synced items by their own time

consequences: Windows FFI can't be compiled on the macOS dev box (reqwest's ring/aws-lc build scripts need the MSVC toolchain, and cross-check fails), so the Windows path is verified by building on the Windows test PC. Linux still has no secret store, so the sync stays off there.
context: The sync was macOS-only solely because the sign-in store (platform::secret_*) was Keychain-only; everything else (native-messaging handover, reqwest calls, parsing, writing sources) is cross-platform. User asked to enable Windows.
decision: Implement secret_get/set/delete on Windows via Credential Manager (CredReadW/CredWriteW/CredDeleteW, a generic credential keyed '<service>/<account>', DPAPI per user) in platform/other.rs behind cfg(windows); Linux keeps the no-store stub. Frontend gates (Settings pane, Today meetings card, Sources Sync now) switch from isMac to a new platform.hasSync = isMac || isWindows. Docs/help/MCP wording changed from 'macOS only' to 'macOS and Windows'.
title: Teams and Outlook sync works on Windows too (Credential Manager)

consequences: Sources are now living documents for sync-origin captures (extension captures and dropped files stay write-once). Re-ingest of topped-up sources depends on the daily check + refreshStale being on; otherwise files stay complete and the user ingests from Sources' Changed filter. Edits to existing messages aren't detected (only growth). Supersedes D-20261025-02's chat-per-day-frozen and mail-per-message behaviour.
context: User wants a new chat message to update the day's source already written, and a new email to update the thread already written, rather than freezing (supersedes the per-day-written-once and per-message parts of D-20261025-02). Chose: whole-conversation threads (incl. sent replies); throttle re-ingest to about daily.
decision: webcapture::rewrite() overwrites an existing source in place (atomic, same name). Chats: one source per chat per day, rewritten in place whenever that day gains messages (state tracks message count per conv/day; days written before counts existed adopt their count once without a rewrite); the quiet-3h/day-over gate is gone. Mail: one source per email thread keyed by Outlook ConversationId — an Inbox message flags its thread, the whole conversation is fetched across folders (so the user's own replies are included), written as a multi-message Outlook capture, and rewritten in place when it grows. Top-ups don't fire a capture event, so they don't re-ingest on arrival; the file becomes 'changed since cited' and the daily check's 'ingest changed sources again' re-ingests it (~daily) — the throttle the user chose. New sources still ingest on arrival. pull_teams_outlook matches (thread-grouped mail, chat/thread top-up/vend).
title: Synced chats and mail top up in place; mail is one source per thread

consequences: The sync works only while Teams is open in the browser (which the user keeps open all day); once the handed-over tokens expire after Teams is closed a while, the pane reads Not signed in until Teams is reopened — no more ~24h unattended window. Upside: Brainstead never mints its own tokens, so its access never exceeds the browser's and it sidesteps tenant token-protection. Refines D-20261025-01.
context: On the user's tenant, tokens the app minted via the OAuth refresh-token grant were rejected (401 from authsvc/outlook) once the handed-over page tokens expired, while the browser's own tokens worked. Likely Conditional Access / token protection rejecting non-browser-minted tokens — the employer-policy risk flagged at the outset.
decision: Drop the refresh-token grant entirely. auth::token(svc) returns a cached handed-over token only while unexpired, else an error telling the user to keep Teams open; it never mints tokens. The Teams extension hands the page's live tokens over more often (every 15 min, was 30) so cached tokens stay fresh while Teams is open (v1.1.5). 'Signed in' now means at least one unexpired token is held. refresh()/GrantResponse/token_endpoint/Service::scope removed; refresh_token still stored only as a handover marker.
title: Sync uses only the browser's handed-over tokens; no app-side token refresh

consequences: Each recurring sitting is captured once under its own date; a sitting with no transcript yet waits instead of inheriting a previous one. Non-recurring meetings are unaffected (one occurrence, one window).
context: A recurring Teams meeting's whole series shares one MeetingThreadId. The transcript sync keyed 'already done' on that thread id and matched Substrate transcripts by it, taking the newest, which pulled an earlier sitting's transcript for a meeting whose own wasn't ready and dated it by the current occurrence.
decision: Identify a transcript by occurrence, not by series: parse_transcript selects the item whose RecordingStartDateTime falls in the occurrence's window (ev.start-1h..ev.end+6h) and returns None otherwise; transcript state is keyed thread_id + occurrence local day.
title: Sync keys transcripts per meeting occurrence, matched by recording time

consequences: A mis-dated or wrong-occurrence transcript is skipped and shown in Sync now's problems, not filed under the wrong date. Chats and email can't mis-name on update (they top up by stored id to path), so no equivalent is needed there. Cross-capture duplicates (same meeting via extension and sync) remain a separate, unbuilt vault-level check.
context: After keying transcripts per occurrence (D-20261026-02), a cheap sentinel was wanted so any future mis-dating of a transcript is surfaced rather than silently written, as the recurring-meeting bug did.
decision: parse_transcript returns Result<Option<Capture>>: after selecting the in-window transcript it compares that transcript's own RecordingStartDateTime day to the occurrence day, and on disagreement returns Err — the sync reports it as a pass problem and does not deliver or mark the meeting done.
title: Sync flags a transcript whose recording day disagrees with the meeting's day

consequences: Threads synced before this get their older messages' attachments when they next grow. A possible later route for chat files: the extension downloads with the browser's SharePoint session and passes the bytes over native messaging (needs a sharepoint.com host permission); not built.
context: User asked (2026-10-26) for email attachments to be brought in as sources and linked from the thread, so an agent reading the thread can find them. A sample of 327 real attachments over four months had one over 25 MB (26.7 MB) and none over 30 MB. A spike showed the Teams page holds no usable SharePoint sign-in (only stale leftovers, none minted on opening a file), so files shared in chats can't be downloaded with handed-over tokens.
decision: Settings switch Bring in email attachments (syncMailAttachments), on by default. Non-inline file attachments ingest can read (pdf, docx, pptx, xlsx, txt, md; not images) up to 30 MB are downloaded once (state keyed by thread + message received time + name, since Outlook ids change on folder moves), written as 'Email. Attachment. <name> - <day>.<ext>' via webcapture::write_file and noted like a capture (Inbox, ingest on arrival). Each message in the thread source gets an **Attachments:** list linking [[sources/<file>|<name>]] by full vault path; inline pictures are omitted; other attachments are listed by name with why. A trashed attachment isn't fetched again. pull_teams_outlook does the same. Teams: files shared in chats are listed under their message as links to OneDrive/SharePoint, not downloaded.
title: Sync brings email attachments into sources/; Teams chat files are links only

consequences: A source renamed outside Brainstead gets a duplicate on its next new message (preferred to silently losing mail). A restored old source and the fresh one can both exist.
context: User pointed out (2026-10-26) that ignoring a trashed thread's later mail is confusing: a thread ingested then trashed would silently drop replies. Asked about the Trash being emptied too. Chose a fresh source over restoring the old one, and the same rule for chat days.
decision: When a synced chat day or email thread gains messages and its source file is no longer at its path, for any reason (trashed, Trash emptied, deleted or renamed outside Brainstead), the sync writes a fresh source with the whole day or thread; it lands in the Inbox and ingests as new, and state points at the new file. Attachments already brought in are linked again (not re-downloaded); a removed attachment is listed as removed. Supersedes the skip-while-trashed behaviour of commit 11edf6b.
title: Sync: new messages on a removed chat day or thread start a fresh source

consequences: A background Teams tab may reload roughly hourly, driven by the one-hour transcripts token; whether a reload renews that token is to be confirmed in use. Extension 1.1.7.
context: The sync went stale again (2026-10-27). Handed-over chat/mail tokens last about 21 hours, the transcripts (substrate) token about 1 hour; Teams renews a token only when it next needs it, and Chrome's Memory Saver can put a background Teams tab to sleep, after which nothing can be read from it. User agreed the plan.
decision: On each hand-over the extension sets the Teams tab autoDiscardable=false. If a token the sync uses (chats, mail, transcripts, channel list) is missing or runs out within 10 minutes, or the tab is asleep, it reloads the tab and hands over a minute later; never a tab that is active in a focused window or audible (a call), and at most once per 45 minutes (chrome.storage.local). Freshness logic in sign-in-freshness.js with a Vitest test. Settings' Sign-in card and the sync MCP tool name the stale services (SignInState.stale).
title: Teams extension keeps the tab's sign-in fresh by reloading a background Teams tab

consequences: A missed reload after an update is visible within one handover. Extensions older than 1.1.8 always read as outdated, which is correct.
context: Chrome loads the Teams extension unpacked and only picks up updated files when it's reloaded, so after an update Chrome kept running 1.1.6 all day without the keep-fresh code and the sign-in went stale.
decision: The extension (1.1.8) sends its manifest version with each sign-in handover; the app keeps it with the sign-in and compares it with the version this build ships (read from the bundled manifest at compile time). When older, or missing because the extension predates 1.1.8, the Settings Sign-in card and MCP teams_sync get ask the user to reload it at chrome://extensions.
title: Settings warns when Chrome runs an older Teams extension

consequences: Depends on MSAL's cache format (cookie msal.cache.encryption, HKDF-SHA256 nonce/clientId, AES-GCM zero IV); a format change shows in the hand-over record (decrypted 0 or a problem) rather than silently.
context: Teams moved to a newer MSAL that keeps tokens encrypted in localStorage, with the key in a page cookie; the hand-over then carried only stale plain leftovers.
decision: readSignIn decrypts the entries inside the Teams page with the page's own key and hands over the same access tokens as before; when any decrypt, plain entries are ignored as leftovers. Nothing new leaves the browser except those access tokens, as before.
title: Teams extension decrypts Teams' encrypted MSAL cache in the page

consequences: Mail sync needs Outlook on the web open in Chrome as well as Teams. Chats, transcripts and channels still come only from Teams.
context: After Teams moved to its newer sign-in cache, the Teams page stopped reliably keeping an Outlook token that can read mail, and opening Calendar in Teams didn't fetch one, so mail sync stalled with 'Gone stale: mail'.
decision: The Outlook extension (1.1.0) hands over an open Outlook on the web tab's sign-in every 15 minutes, using the same page reader as the Teams extension (sign-in-reader.js, a copy in each kept identical by a test). The app takes only the Outlook mail token from it (auth::with_mail_handover); a Teams hand-over keeps live tokens for services it lacks (auth::keep_missing). The Teams extension no longer reloads its tab for a missing mail token.
title: Mail's token comes from the Outlook extension

consequences: The main window's chrome is the app's on both platforms. Windows 11's snap layouts flyout does not appear over the app's maximise button: Windows offers it only when the window under the pointer answers WM_NCHITTEST with HTMAXBUTTON. A new screen bar needs the drag attribute on its empty space and 156px of right padding on Windows (html[data-platform=windows] .top). Linux is untouched.
context: The Windows port kept the native title bar (commit bdd7aea) while macOS has titleBarStyle Overlay with the app's header carrying the traffic lights, so the two looked different and the Windows header sat under a bar the app did not draw. Tao 0.37 gives an undecorated resizable window the DWM frame, resize borders (top edge itself, the others through tauri-runtime-wry's child window over the webview), Alt+F4, Win+arrow snapping, and clamps a maximised one to the work area; WebView2's window belongs to another process, so the main window is never asked WM_NCHITTEST for points over the page.
decision: tauri.windows.conf.json sets decorations false and shadow true for the main window. src/WindowControls.tsx draws minimise, maximise and close at the top right, 46 by 32 like the native ones, Windows only (isWindows); close calls the window's close(), which emits CloseRequested, so lib.rs hides or quits with the unsaved-edits question as for the native X. dragRegion() returns the attribute on macOS and Windows (Linux keeps its title bar); it goes on a bar's empty space only, and the top bar's spacer too.
title: Windows main window has no native title bar

consequences: Clicks and the tooltip on the maximise button belong to the child window, not the page. If a WebView2 or Windows update changes how the flyout is triggered, this commit can be reverted alone; the rest of the borderless window does not depend on it.
context: Windows 11 shows its snap-layouts flyout over a maximise button only to a window that answers WM_NCHITTEST with HTMAXBUTTON. The page's button is drawn by WebView2, whose window belongs to another process, so the main window is never asked for points over it. Tauri solves the same problem for resize borders with a child window of its own (tauri-runtime-wry undecorated_resizing).
decision: platform/snap_win.rs puts a child window of the app's process over the maximise button that answers HTMAXBUTTON, paints nothing, maximises or restores the main window on button release (SC_MAXIMIZE or SC_RESTORE), and emits window-controls-hover so the page shows the button hovered. src/WindowControls.tsx places it through the window_max_button command, in physical pixels, on resize and scale change, and removes it on unmount. Non-client mouse moves still reach DefWindowProc, where the system's flyout handling runs.
title: Snap layouts over the app's maximise button on Windows

consequences: The controls line up with the bar's own buttons. The snap-layout child window follows the button's size, since the page sends the button's rect. Changing the bar's height means changing --top-h only.
context: The first version drew minimise, maximise and close 46 by 32 like Windows' native caption buttons, so on the 52px top bar their glyphs sat above the bar's centre line and the hover shade was a short box. Angus preferred the look of Claude's desktop app on Windows, whose buttons are as tall as its header.
decision: Each button is 46px wide and as tall as the top bar above its divider (calc(var(--top-h) - 1px), with --top-h the bar's height, now a :root variable the bar and the help drawer use too), the glyph centred, the hover and pressed shades filling the whole button, close in Windows red.
title: Windows window controls fill the top bar
